content.text:
I'm weighing a candidate point about the preamble's proxy-rule wording for employees with one or two ratings, but the regulation text for a single rating actually calls for multiplying by three, so it's a borderline characterization and I'm leaning toward dropping it. Now I'm moving on to the Q12 analysis, starting with the October 5 notice.

Now I'm working through the Q12 employee-by-employee calculations under the new rules, with no cutoff since the notice is dated October 5, 2026. For each employee I'm totaling the ratings within the four-year window, applying the proxy where it's needed, and noting the subgroup and service computation date. Chen's Level 2 rating from September 30, 2022 falls just outside that window, so only two of his ratings count.

I'm checking Farouk's restoration protection, which runs until July 2027 and makes his placement mandatory, and I'm noting that Quinn is still in her initial probation so she isn't a competing employee and can be retained. With the totals in, the ranking comes out as Alvarez 19, then Chen and Dube at 18 (Chen ahead on subgroup), Estrada 16, Brandt 13, and Farouk 9, with Quinn left unranked.

I'm settling on three releases: Brandt, Estrada, and Dube, since Farouk's restoration protection makes him a mandatory exception while another competing employee can be released instead, and Quinn stays as a non-competing employee. I also checked the December 4 effective date against Farouk's one-year restoration protection running to July 2027, and it still covers that date.

Now I'm checking the assignment rights for each released employee. Brandt's current rating of record is Level 2 from November 2025, so he qualifies, and Dube's is Level 4. Estrada qualifies either way, since her rating of record is at least Level 2.

I'm now listing the holders for the GS-12 through GS-9 positions, since the one-grade interval for this RIF reaches down to GS-9 for Brandt and that's what I'm working out. For each holder I'm totaling the performance credit, adding subgroup and service computation date, to set their retention standing.

Gomez's GS-12 sits above Hill's GS-11 and Jones's GS-10 in retention standing, so Dube's 18 puts her ahead of all three and she gets offered the GS-12 slot first. For Estrada, the GS-11 position goes to Hill, whose 14 is the lower standing, which means the smallest reduction. I still need to check what happens to Gomez once Dube takes his position.

I'm checking the remaining positions against each displaced employee's assignment rights, starting with the order of processing by retention standing. Once Gomez, Hill, and Ikeda are displaced, I'll see whether any of them can bump into a position they qualify for.

I'm checking whether the separated employees could qualify for any other position, and since each of Gomez, Hill, and Ikeda only qualifies for the position they hold, they're separated. I'm also confirming that the GS-13 displacement rule applies here.

I'm noting that Estrada's October 20 rating came after the notice, so it doesn't change the rating-of-record question, and Gomez, Hill, and Ikeda end up separated since each only qualifies for the position they already hold. Next I'm working through the dates for the Q4 notice, starting with the 4-year window that runs from September 3, 2022 to September 2, 2026.

I'm figuring the three most recent ratings for the Q4 employee: the August 2026 Level 5 counts as 7, and the November 2025 and November 2024 Level 3s add 3 each, so the total comes to 13. Next I'm working out the 45-day cutoff before September 3, 2026, counting back through August and July to land on July 20.

I'm checking the cutoff for the Q4 employee: the August 10 rating falls after July 20, 2026, so it's excluded. Over the four years before that cutoff, the three most recent ratings are 3, 3, and 4, which gives 11. I'm also ruling out the July 15 rating, since it wasn't on record until August 15, after the cutoff, so it can't be used.

Now I'm working out Hank's standing: he has no rating of record in the four-year window, so his performance credit would come from the modal rating for his position's summary level pattern. I'm also noting that the modal value isn't spelled out in what I have, and I'm moving on to Q3 to check whether the Lt Col qualifies as preference eligible.

I'm checking the Commander's case: as an O-5, a major-equivalent, he'd only be preference eligible with a disability that also meets one of the retirement conditions, and his retirement is length-based, so he isn't, leaving him with no points in Subgroup B. Now I'm moving to the Major's disability retirement from armed conflict at 60%, which meets the first retirement condition, so I'm checking the major-or-above rule next.

I'm assessing the staff sergeant's case: his medical retirement after 16 years meets the length-of-service condition, and since he isn't a major or above, that rule doesn't apply, so he's preference eligible with a 10% disability that falls under the 30% threshold, giving him 3 points.

I'm working out the seniority date for the retired member: he only gets campaign-time credit since he isn't preference eligible, which puts his date at September 7, 2008. The other employee, who is preference eligible, gets full active service credit, putting their date at September 7, 1996.

I'm checking whether the campaign-only credit for the retired member is right under 351.505(b)(2), since "covered by 351.504(b)" could be read loosely, but the more defensible reading gives him two years, so his date stays at September 7, 2008. I'm also confirming the subgroup labels don't change the order, since retention is set by performance credit plus points first, then tenure subgroup, then service computation date.

Next I'm checking the Q6 case: Jordan's GS-13 has a one-grade interval, so the only positions in range are GS-12, GS-11, and GS-10, and Ellis, Frank, and Gale all qualify. Ito's higher standing and the part-time and different-competitive-area positions rule themselves out, so the offer has to go to whichever of the three keeps the representative rate least reduced, which is the GS-12 slot held by Ellis. For the 30% disabled case, the interval stretches to five grades, which brings GS-9 Hana into range.

I'm checking Jordan's case once more: a Level 1 current rating means no assignment rights under 351.701(a), which requires Level 2 or higher, so the likely outcome is separation or furlough. I'm also noting that excepted service employees only get assignment rights if the agency adopted the provisions under 351.705(a), and I still need to look at the 2026 preamble on the Level 2 restriction.

I'm checking the MSPB rule's effective-date language for appeals received after September 2, since it seems to cover RIFs whose effective date came before that, while the OPM appeals rule doesn't reach this notice.

I'm checking the MSPB versus OPM question against the notice dates: the Morgan RIF's October 30 effective date conflicts with the MSPB rule's September 2 cutoff, so I'll flag that and lean toward MSPB. For the October 19 notice, the filing goes through OPM's electronic system, and the 30-day window starts December 19 and ends January 17, 2027.

I'm checking whether January 17, 2027 is a Sunday, which would push the deadline forward to the next workday, and I'm noticing that Monday the 18th may be a federal holiday, so I need to confirm the calendar before settling the deadline.

Now I'm working out the burden for the appeal: the employee has to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the appeal is timely, that it falls within jurisdiction, that the agency failed to follow the statute or OPM rules governing the RIF, and that this caused harm to them.

I'm now going through the remaining Q7 points: grievance and arbitration are barred under the RIF appeal rules, so I need to check the preamble's discussion of existing collective bargaining agreements. I'm also noting that judicial review isn't available, and I'm looking at whether the preamble's constitutional discussion changes anything.

I'm working out that April 9, 2027 falls on a Friday, so it's a workday and needs no extension. I'm also noting caveats: OPM decides whether the action "materially affects" retention in its sole discretion, and an OSC complaint usually doesn't produce a final decision correcting a rating, which typically comes through MSPB corrective action.

I'm settling the applicability question: the rule's DATES language ties it to RIF notices issued on or after September 2, 2026, which is the cutoff I need for the Morgan and October 19 cases. Next I'm turning to the Q8 point about the existing 351.806 text, which is still in force today and gets revised effective November 18.

I'm checking the consent question for the leave on Oct 26: neither 351.806(b) nor 630.1403(c)(10) requires the employee's consent, since the decision rests on what the agency finds appropriate. The contrast is with emergency annual leave and leave without pay, which do turn on consent, and the leave-in-place authority is limited to the period between receipt of the RIF notice and the RIF's effective date.

I'm checking the consent question for the leave on Oct 26 against 351.806 and 630.1403, and the governing 12-week limit seems to apply only to workforce realignment initiatives, so it's unclear whether it reaches this notice-period leave. I'm also setting aside the investigative 10-workday limit in 6329a since it doesn't apply here, and moving on to how OPM's 2025 policy guidance treated authorized administrative leave.

I'm noting that the preamble says the provisions don't change the substantive or procedural RIF rules, so nothing there lets an agency skip retention registers or appeal rights, and standing is still fixed when the notice is received. I'm also checking the Q9 timeline: the competitive area was set on August 17 and the notices went out October 13, which is 57 days later and inside the 90-day window, so the agency has to send OPM the description and written statement.

Now I'm checking the Q9 steps against the regulations: the competitive area was set on August 17 and notices went out October 13, so that's within the 90-day window and the agency owes OPM a description and written statement in advance, which wasn't done. Novak's probation keeps her out of the competing group, but Ortiz's supervisory probation doesn't count as an initial probationary period, so she has to be on the register. The performance cutoff falls on September 13, and Ortiz's October 2 rating comes after it, so it can't be used.

I'm checking the remaining Q9 points against the proxy rule: two ratings of 5 and 4 average to 6, which gives 18 rather than 15, so that's out of compliance. The additional credit isn't allowed either, since the single five-level pattern doesn't fit the Level 3 or multiple-pattern exceptions. Reyes's temporary promotion means she can't be released while a competing employee with a limited temporary promotion at that level is retained.

I'm checking Silva's exemption under the five-year window ending October 13, 2026: he held the same position with a Level 4 rating in 2022, so that falls within the window and he's covered. The self-rating questionnaire is scored automatically, which conflicts with the rule against relying solely or mainly on automated self-assessment and with the job analysis requirement, so that's out of compliance too. For Tran, she's been given 60 days under one exception and then another 60 under a second, but stacking them isn't allowed and the second exception caps at 90 days anyway, so that's not compliant.

I'm checking the remaining Q9 points: the notices went out on October 13, 2026, so the OPM appeal rules apply rather than MSPB, and 351.802(a)(6) requires the OPM appeal right and filing system. Then I'm moving to Q10, looking at what paragraph (1) of "displaced" contained on September 10 before instruction 11 of 2026-15665 revised it.

I'm checking the paragraph (1) wording that was in place on September 10, which only had the introductory text until the September 15 correction restored subparagraphs (i) and (ii). For the displaced-status question, I'm reading (1)(i) on its own: an employee who received a RIF separation notice and hasn't declined an equal-rate, same-schedule offer stays displaced, while turning down a lower-rate offer doesn't change that.

I'm noting that Nadia got her RIF notice on September 8, which falls in the gap between September 2 and September 15, so the displaced definition as it stood then may not have covered her. Next I'm checking the other 2026 final rules that amend part 351: one on RIF appeals effective September 2, and two more effective November 18 that aren't in force yet.

I'm checking whether the 2026 final rule that touches part 351 changes anything in that part, and I'm still to look at the November 18 rule and see whether it amends 351 at all, plus the earlier August 6 performance appraisal rule, which falls outside the September 2 cutoff.

  1934  Sec.  351.902  Procedures for submitting appeals.
  1935  
  1936      (a) Filing an appeal. A party, or his or her authorized 
  1937  representative, seeking to file an initial appeal or reconsideration of 
  1938  an initial appeal under this part must utilize the electronic filing 
  1939  (e-filing) system available at [URL TBD]. Unless a party demonstrates 
  1940  good cause and seeks approval from OPM, OPM will not accept any 
  1941  statements, evidence, or documents via electronic mail or postal mail.
  1942      (b) Time limits. An employee may submit an appeal of a reduction in 
  1943  force action within 30 calendar days from the effective date of the 
  1944  action. An appeal is deemed timely when it is electronically filed by 
  1945  11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on the 30th calendar day after the 
  1946  effective date of the action.
  1947      (1) In computing the number of days allowed for filing an appeal, 
  1948  the first day counted is the day after the effective date of an Agency 
  1949  action. If the date that ordinarily would be the last day for filing 
  1950  falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday, the filing period will 
  1951  include the first workday after that date.
  1952      (2) If an employee does not submit an appeal within the time set by 
  1953  this section, the appeal will be dismissed as untimely filed unless the 
  1954  employee demonstrates good cause for an untimely appeal.
  1955      (3) The determination of good cause will be in the sole and 
  1956  exclusive discretion of OPM.
  1957      (c) E-filing procedures.
  1958      (1) All parties and their representatives to an appeal or 
  1959  reconsideration must register as instructed by OPM on its e-filing 
  1960  system using a unique email address.
  1961      (2) Registration as an e-filer constitutes consent to accept 
  1962  electronic service of pleadings, evidence, notices, orders, and other 
  1963  documents filed by other e-filers or issued by OPM. No party may 
  1964  electronically file any document with OPM or access an appeal or 
  1965  reconsideration of an appeal unless registered as an e-filer.
  1966      (3) All notices, orders, decisions, and other documents issued by 
  1967  OPM, as well as all documents filed by parties, will be made available 
  1968  for viewing and downloading at OPM's electronic filing system. Access 
  1969  to documents is limited to the parties and their representatives who 
  1970  are registered e-filers in the cases in which they were filed.
  1971      (4) All parties and their representatives must follow the 
  1972  instructions on OPM's website for properly filing all pleadings, 
  1973  evidence, and other documents. OPM may issue orders regulating the 
  1974  method and form of submissions and sanctions for noncompliance, 
  1975  including ordering any party or authorized individual to cease 
  1976  participation as an e-filer in circumstances that constitute a misuse 
  1977  of the system or a failure to comply with law, rule, regulations, or 
  1978  policy governing the use of a U.S. government information system.
  1979      (5) Each e-filer must promptly update their profile in OPM's 
  1980  electronic filing system and notify OPM and other parties of any change 
  1981  in their best address, telephone number, or email address by filing a 
  1982  pleading in each pending case with which they are associated. E-filers 
  1983  are responsible for monitoring case activity regularly in OPM's 
  1984  electronic filing system to ensure that they have received all case-
  1985  related documents.

  1987  e-filer pursuant to the requirements posted on OPM's website.

  1993  through OPM's e-filing system. OPM may still process an appeal or 
  1994  request for reconsideration after a party withdraws as an e-filer. 
  1995  Withdrawal as a party or party's representative will not be considered 
  1996  good cause for staying a case. As the e-file system is the only 
  1997  accepted method for filing an appeal, a withdrawal of registration as 
  1998  an e-filer may preclude future re-registering as an e-filer.
  1999      (7) OPM, in its sole and exclusive discretion, may exempt a party 
  2000  or representative from registering as an e-filer for good cause. A 
  2001  party or representative must promptly contact OPM as instructed on

  2004  appeal or seek reconsideration if the party or representative fails to

  2061  representative when the representative is an employee of the

  2069  Sec.  351.905  Adjudication of appeals.
  2070  
  2071      (a) Appeals by non-OPM employees. OPM will assign personnel to 
  2072  adjudicate an appeal under this subpart by an employee of an agency 
  2073  other than OPM. However, no OPM employee may be assigned to adjudicate 
  2074  an appeal if the employee has a relationship with the appellant 
  2075  employee or, during the preceding two years, that person was an 
  2076  employee of the agency that is a party to the action to be assigned, or

  2081  judge to adjudicate an appeal under this subpart by an OPM employee. To 
  2082  insulate the adjudication of its own employees' appeals from agency 
  2083  involvement, OPM will not disturb initial decisions in those cases 
  2084  unless a party shows that there has been harmful procedural 
  2085  irregularity in the proceedings before the administrative law judge or 
  2086  a clear error of law. For these purposes, the term harmful procedural 
  2087  irregularity means an irregularity in the application of procedures was 
  2088  likely to have caused the administrative law judge to reach a 
  2089  conclusion different from the one he or she would have reached in the

  2091      (c) Ascertainment of facts. OPM may audit or investigate an 
  2092  agency's reduction in force action in the course of adjudicating an 
  2093  appeal if it determines, in its sole and exclusive discretion, the 
  2094  interest of justice is served by such an audit or investigation. The 
  2095  review of an agency action will be based solely on the developed 
  2096  written record unless OPM determines that a hearing or any other 
  2097  appropriate action is necessary and efficient to resolve an appeal and 
  2098  directs the parties to participate in such hearing or comply with such 
  2099  action. For purposes of this section, the term necessary and efficient 
  2100  means circumstances in which the written record is insufficiently 
  2101  developed to make a determination regarding one or more facts material 
  2102  to the outcome of the appeal, or where there is a disputed issue of 
  2103  witness credibility that is material to the outcome of the appeal. 
  2104  Where an investigation or audit is conducted, OPM will:
  2105      (1) Inform the employee, the employee's representative, and the 
  2106  agency of an investigation or audit; and
  2107      (2) Provide the employee, the employee's representative, and the 
  2108  agency with the results of an investigation or audit, and a reasonable 
  2109  opportunity to submit arguments or additional information to support 
  2110  their positions.
  2111      (d) Failure to participate in ascertainment of facts. If a party 
  2112  fails to participate in an audit or investigation pursuant to 
  2113  351.905(c), OPM may, except when prohibited by law, impose any sanction 
  2114  listed at 351.906(b)(1)-(3).
  2115      (e) Initial decision. OPM will notify the employee, employee's 
  2116  representative, and agency in writing of its decision.

  2118  order relief including correction of the personnel action and any back 
  2119  pay, interest, and reasonable attorney fees consistent with subpart H 
  2120  of part 550 of this chapter. The employee as a prevailing party is not 
  2121  entitled to compensatory damages or other relief not authorized under 5 
  2122  U.S.C. 5596(b).
  2123      (2) If the agency timely requests reconsideration of an initial 
  2124  decision or OPM reopens and reconsiders an initial decision, the agency 
  2125  must continue to provide the relief ordered unless OPM issues an order 
  2126  staying any such relief. No such stay may be ordered that would deprive 
  2127  pay and benefits to the employee while the initial decision is pending 
  2128  reconsideration.

  2131  Sec.  351.906  Sanctions and protective orders.
  2132  
  2133      (a) Cease-and-desist directive. OPM may issue a directive to a 
  2134  party to prevent or to cease-and-desist harassing communications (or 
  2135  communications which could reasonably be foreseen to lead to 
  2136  harassment) with or about any individual, or to prohibit a party from 
  2137  using any information related to the appeal for any purpose whatsoever 
  2138  unrelated to the adjudication of the appeal. OPM may do this sua 
  2139  sponte, or at the request of a party, preemptively or at any juncture 
  2140  in the appeal process. A party requesting OPM to issue a protective 
  2141  order or cease-and-desist should file such request using the e-filing

  2143  of reasons justifying the request, together with any relevant 
  2144  documentary evidence.
  2145      (b) Failure to comply with an OPM directive. When a party to an 
  2146  appeal fails to comply with a directive issued under paragraph (a), OPM 
  2147  shall, except when prohibited by law:
  2148      (1) Draw all inferences in opposition to the noncompliant party 
  2149  with regard to the appeal in question;
  2150      (2) Prohibit the noncompliant party from introducing evidence, or 
  2151  additional evidence, concerning the appeal, or otherwise relying on the 
  2152  record; or
  2153      (3) Eliminate from consideration any appropriate part of the 
  2154  filings or other submissions of the noncompliant party.
  2155  
  2156  
  2157  Sec.  351.907  Reconsideration of an initial decision.
  2158  
  2159      (a) Upon a request from either party to the dispute, OPM may, in 
  2160  its sole and
  2161  
  2162  [[Page 5877]]
  2163  
  2164  exclusive discretion, reopen and reconsider an initial decision issued 
  2165  under this subpart. An employee, the employee's representative, or the 
  2166  agency may request reopening and reconsideration of an initial decision 
  2167  within 30 calendar days from issuance of the initial decision. The 
  2168  request to reopen and reconsider must be filed in the same manner as an 
  2169  initial appeal.
  2170      (b) Grounds for which OPM may grant a request for reconsideration 
  2171  are:
  2172      (1) The initial decision contains erroneous findings of material 
  2173  fact sufficient to warrant an outcome different from that of the 
  2174  initial decision;
  2175      (2) The initial decision is based on an erroneous interpretation of 
  2176  statute or regulation or the erroneous application of the law to the 
  2177  facts of the case. The party must explain how the error affected the 
  2178  outcome of the case;
  2179      (3) New and material evidence or legal argument is available that, 
  2180  despite the party's due diligence, was not available when the record 
  2181  closed. To constitute new evidence, the information contained in the 
  2182  documents, not just the documents themselves, must have been 
  2183  unavailable despite due diligence when the record closed; or
  2184      (4) OPM finds good cause to reconsider an appeal.
  2185      (c) In any case that is reopened or reviewed, OPM may:
  2186      (1) Issue a reopened and reconsidered decision (``R&R decision'') 
  2187  that affirms, reverses, modifies, vacates, or otherwise decides the 
  2188  case, in whole or in part;
  2189      (2) Require the parties to submit argument and evidence;
  2190      (3) Take any other action necessary for final disposition of the 
  2191  case; and
  2192      (4) Issue an order with a date for compliance with the R&R 
  2193  decision.
  2194      (d) There is no further right of administrative appeal from the R&R 
  2195  decision.

  2214      (c) A decision by the Director pursuant to Sec.  351.908 is the

content.text:
I'm checking the final appeals rule against the proposal for changes it doesn't acknowledge. The proposal listed FLRA among the preserved jurisdictions, but the final rule drops it, and the summary doesn't mention that removal. The proposal's language that it would supersede appeal procedures in agency policies and collective bargaining agreements is also gone, and the summary doesn't say so.

I'm comparing the remaining changes against the proposal: the final rule also drops the MSPB notice requirement from 351.802(a)(6), and the summary only mentions the added time-limit and e-filing information. Several smaller wording changes in 351.902, 351.905(a), and 351.905(c) are either barely noted or not noted at all.

I'm going through the rest of the unacknowledged changes. The proposal's "OPM shall" in 351.906(b) became "OPM may," and a new proportionality paragraph (c) appeared, but the summary only covers paragraph (a). A few smaller wording shifts in 351.902(a), 351.902(c)(2), and 351.907(a) also go unmentioned, while the concerned-party and withdrawal changes in 351.909 and 351.902(c)(6) are already noted.

I'm checking the remaining preamble claims against the reg text: the summary says the final text keeps the sole-and-exclusive-means language, but the reg changes "this part" to "this subpart", and the summary doesn't mention that wording shift. The other notes there (the 30-day finality, the inspection and service changes, the simplified initial-appeal information) look accurate as stated.

I'm checking the preamble's tolling note against the reg text, which was corrected to point at paragraph (c)(3) instead. I also want to confirm the RIF notice citation, since the 351.802 reference may belong to 351.801.

I'm going to check the section-by-section text for any remaining mismatches, searching for specific terms like the FLRA reference, the 1201.21 citation, and the deadline wording, since reading the whole stretch would take too much of my remaining room.

I'm checking the preamble's wording against the regulation: the preamble says the appellant must prove the written appeal was timely and in the required form, but the regulation text only mentions timeliness, so that's a real difference in substance. I'm also noting that the applicability language ties back to the RIF rule's effective date, which happens to fall on the same day, though that alone doesn't make it a discrepancy.

I'm also checking whether the procedures cited in the preamble ("part 351") line up with the corrected "this subpart," which looks like a trivial wording difference. Next I'll go through the section-by-section discussion for 351.902 and 351.903 to look for other mismatches, such as the reply period and the agency response.

content.text:
I'm checking the OPM rule's section-by-section note on reopening appeals against the regulation text, and they're close enough that I'll skip it. I have what I need for Q14, so I'm moving on to the MSPB rule inconsistencies, starting with the dates issue in the 51997 rule.

Now I'm comparing the MSPB rule's date language against the other sections, since the notice date and the effective date seem to point in different directions. I'm also noting that the APA good-cause claim sits awkwardly next to the September 2 effective date.

I'm checking the 2026-17335 correction notice, which fixes clerical errors in the amendatory instructions and regulatory text and has its own docket number that differs from the main rule's. I'm also noting the 2026-18800 correction that restores the "displaced" wording in 330.602, then I'll weigh the minor proviso difference in the proposed versus final 351.202(d)(3) text.

I'm pulling the citation details for the main OPM rule, which runs from page 49178 to 49227 and takes effect September 2, 2026, and I'm noting the docket and RIN. I'm also checking the earlier proposed rule's publication date and comment deadline, and I'm moving on to how amended notices that only change the effective date are treated.

I'm working out the timing rules for this RIF case: the 4-year period ends at the date the RIF notices were issued, not the date of the final rule, and the Oct 15 rating falls outside it. Since no error was made, the correction duty doesn't apply, so Lee is still released. For the Sept 2 notice, the new rules apply, and I'm tallying Lee's retention points at 9 and Park's at 21.

Lee's case falls under the earlier rules in this alternative, and both employees are career employees in the same tenure subgroup. Adjusting their service dates for veterans' preference, Lee's adjusted date comes out earlier than Park's, so Lee would be retained and Park released. I'm also noting that the four-year lookback period for this cutoff runs from July 20, 2022 to July 20, 2026.

I'm checking the 4-year lookback against the cutoff date, which works out to September 13, 2026 for the Oct 13 cutoff, and I'm tallying the 11 points from the three most recent ratings. Then I'll check the step 1 timing and whether the action counts as "establishing" the designation, followed by the five-year window and Silva's compliance.

I'm noting that the 2026 appeals rule requires the notice to state the filing time limit and the e-filing system, and that the 30-day window is right but the forum is wrong. Next I'm checking Eze's four-year term appointment from 2023, which falls under the competitive-service term rules in part 316 subpart C and places her in subgroup II.

I'm looking at how the final rule worded the disclosure of performance credit in 351.506(c), since the singular phrasing may limit what's shown to the employee, even though the preamble just calls it a consistency change. I'm also noting that the order of offers requires the agency to place the employee in the position needing the least reduction, which here is GS-12 Ellis, not any of the three. Then I'll check how Q6(b)'s 30% disability rating would add 5 points and possibly shift the standings.

Next I'm going through the remaining points on the 351.701 assignment rights and the excepted-service discretion under 351.705. I'm also checking the formula for creditable service in 351.505(d)(2) and noting that Chen's Level 2 rating from September 30, 2022 falls just before the four-year period begins on October 5, 2022.

I'm checking the stated exception for Farouk, who was restored on July 13, 2026 after 14 months of uniformed service, so he's protected and Dube is released instead. Then I'm weighing Gomez, Estrada, Hill, Brandt, and Ikeda against the GS-12 and GS-9 openings to see who can take each one.

I'm finishing the Brandt check, since GS-9 sits within his five-grade limit, and then I'm noting that Dube's displacement of Gomez falls within the same competitive tenure group. Next I'm sorting the outcomes for the GS-13 group: Gomez, Hill, and Ikeda are separated with no assignment rights, Jones keeps her place, Alvarez, Chen, Farouk, and Quinn stay at GS-13, and Dube, Estrada, and Brandt are demoted.

I'm listing the exceptions for temporary appointments of one year or less, comparing the executive summary and preamble wording against the regulation's narrower reference to subpart D of part 316 for competitive service.

I'm cross-checking the regulation's 5-year window for RIF assessments against the executive summary's wording, which says "within five years of the RIF," and the reg's version keyed to the RIF notice date. I'm also comparing the preamble's description of automated self-assessments with the reg's narrower "solely or principally" language, since the executive summary doesn't cover that point.

I'm checking a possible mismatch in Section 351.705: the preamble says the old paragraph (c) is being kept and renumbered, but the amendatory instruction only revises paragraph (a). I'm flagging it as a likely discrepancy worth including, and then I'm moving on to the changes to the conforming provisions in item 5.

I'm going through the remaining items: the 351.805 successive-notice point, which I'll skip since it only covers amended notices, and the FOIA and Privacy Act point on 351.506(d), which looks consistent. I'm also checking whether the RIF notice requirement for excluded employees matches the regulation, and it mostly does. Last, I'm starting to look at the correction notice's summary, which calls the changes non-substantive even though it touches 351.503(b)(2).

I'm now compiling the Q11 list of excluded-employee provisions, rewording the 351.202(d) introduction so it says these appointments aren't competing employees. I'm also dropping the "as of the date of the RIF notice" timing language from the exclusions in (d)(1)(ii) and (d)(2)(i)-(ii), and I'm working through the temporary-appointment exclusion in (d)(2)(iii).

I'm going through the remaining Q11 items now: the 351.202(d)(3) retention language, which I'm reading as allowing retention only while the competing employee is released and the actions stay consistent with the appointment, plus the 351.203 furlough and rating-of-record changes and the new restoration-protected definition.

I'm now going through the 351.302(d) change, which adds "if applicable, or other procedures required by law" to the reference to part 752, and then checking the 351.502 date changes that switch from when the agency issues a notice to when the employee receives it.

I'm going through the Q11 compilation now, covering the 351.503 rating and level changes and the 351.504 and 351.505 wording shifts.

I'm now going through the remaining Q11 items on the 351.506 and 351.604 to 351.606 provisions, noting that the 351.605 restructuring adds a written notice requirement under 351.801 and drops the retention register. I'm also flagging that the 351.606(a) proposal on retention priorities was changed into a mandatory exception under 353.209(b).

I'm going through the rest of the Q11 compilation, checking the 351.802 changes to the veterans' preference subgroup and the records-access wording, along with the new 351.805(b) provision, and I'm noting one last item on the 351.503(d)(3) and (e)(1) changes.

I'm skipping the trivial wording item and the authority citation, since neither needs comparison. Then I'm moving to the Q14 compilation, comparing the preamble's description of the appeal burden against the reg text, which covers timeliness and form of the written appeal.

I'm checking the preamble's reference to the RIF notice under 351.802 against the regulation, which places notice issuance under 351.801, so I'm treating that as a minor point I can skip. Then I'm moving on to the tolling rule's cross-reference to 351.901(c), which I've confirmed is not a real mismatch, and the exclusivity language, which matches the preserved jurisdiction of the other agencies. Last, I'm confirming that the 351.906(b) "may" wording is consistent between the section-by-section and the reg.

I'm checking the remaining e-filing and sole-discretion wording against the regulation, and those look consistent enough to drop. Of the comparisons in this stretch, only the burden-of-proof point about timeliness and form stands as a real mismatch, so I'm noting that and moving on to the audit language in the supplementary information.

I'm checking the summary's list of preserved jurisdictions, where the FLRA seems to have dropped off between the proposal and the final rule without being mentioned. I'm also weighing whether the deleted "supersede" clause for agency policies and bargaining agreements was really acknowledged by the replacement wording, and I'll keep that one as a tentative point.

I'm noting that the summary leaves out the deleted reference to 1201.21 in 351.802(a)(6), which only the section-by-section discusses. Then I'm checking the 351.906(b) change from "shall" to "may" and the new proportionality paragraph in (c), since the summary only covers (a). I'm also flagging the authority citation additions and the 351.905(c) edits, where the information-request power and the removed "appropriate action" language aren't mentioned.

I'm checking the remaining 351.902 and 351.905 changes against the summary, noting the added exemption reference and the "best address" wording that the summary doesn't mention. The ALJ appointment wording and the 351.903(b) timing are minor enough to set aside, and I'm also noting the MSPB inconsistencies and the related docket references.

I'm now checking the remaining date and effective-status details against the rules, covering the 2026-15666 rule already in force, the two Nov 18 rules that aren't effective yet, and how the rating-of-record changes in 351.203 and 351.503 would affect the leave scenario.

Now I'm checking the effective date of the 2026-15666 rule, which I've confirmed is November 18, and I'm noting that the companion correction conforms the authority citation to the appeals rule.

Now I'm settling the arithmetic: Dalton's proxy comes to 3.5, which brings the total to 13.5.

1. **FLRA dropped.** Proposed § 351.901(c) (91 FR 5875) preserved matters within the jurisdiction of the "Federal Labor Relations Authority" along with EEOC, Inspectors General, MSPB, DOL VETS and OSC. Notices were issued September 3, 2026, so the amended rules apply. The four-year window runs from September 3, 2022 to the notice date. Values: Level 5 = 7, Level 4 = 5, Level 3 = 3, Level 2 or 1 = 0.
(a) Scores:
- **Abbott**: 7+5+5 = 17; no preference, +0; **total 17**. Subgroup I.
- **Bianchi**: 5+0+3 = 8; preference eligible with 30% disability, +5 (Subgroup AD); **total 13**. Subgroup I.
- **Castillo**: 7+5+5 = 17; +0, **total 17**. He is a retired member and not a preference eligible:
  - his retirement is not based on combat or instrumentality-of-war disability (§ 351.504(b)(1));
  - his retired pay is based on 20 or more years of active service, so (b)(2) fails;
  - he has no continuous employment since 1964 ((b)(3));
  - as a lieutenant colonel ("major or above") he would also have to be a disabled veteran ((b)(4)).
  Subgroup B; tenure subgroup I.
- **Dalton**: only two ratings, so a proxy is used (§ 351.503(f)(2)). Proxy = (7+0)/2 = 3.5. Credit = 7+0+3.5 = 10.5; preference eligible, +3 (Subgroup A); **total 13.5**. Subgroup I.
- **Eze**: 5+5+5 = 15; +0; **total 15**. A four-year term appointment is longer than one year, so he is a competing employee in competitive service tenure **subgroup II**: he is not career, not in an initial probationary period, and not on a temporary appointment of one year or less (§ 351.502(a)(3); § 351.202(d)(2)).
- **Fontaine**: one rating, multiplied by three (§ 351.503(f)(3)): 5×3 = 15; +0; **total 15**. Subgroup I.
(b) Order of retention (§ 351.501(b)–(c)):
1. Abbott, 17 (subgroup I, SCD May 1, 2003).
2. Castillo, 17 (subgroup I, SCD August 1, 2012). Tied with Abbott on score and subgroup; Abbott's earlier SCD ranks him higher.
3. Fontaine, 15 (subgroup I).
4. Eze, 15 (subgroup II). Tied with Fontaine; subgroup I comes ahead of subgroup II, so his earlier SCD (2009) does not matter.
5. Dalton, 13.5.
6. Bianchi, 13.
**Released: Bianchi and Dalton.**
(c) Under the earlier rules as the 2026 preamble describes them, **Bianchi would have stood above Abbott**. Both are in tenure group I. Under those rules, veterans' preference subgroup ranked ahead of performance and service: AD before A before B. Performance only added years to the adjusted SCD within a subgroup. Bianchi (AD) would therefore have ranked ahead of Abbott (B) whatever their ratings.
(d) Bianchi has received a specific notice, so she and her representative may inspect the retention registers and related records (§ 351.506(b)(1)). She may review the complete retention register (§ 351.506(c)(1)), which includes:
- her name and the names of all other employees on the register;
- her own performance credit as augmented by veterans' preference;
- her own SCD;
- registers for other positions that affect her competitive level or her assignment rights (§ 351.506(c)(2)).
Access must be consistent with FOIA and the Privacy Act (§ 351.506(e)). The register must also show the reasons for any deviation from the order of release (§ 351.606(c)). Her own notice must state her competitive level, veterans' preference subgroup, tenure group and subgroup, service date and three most recent ratings (§ 351.802(a)(2)).
